title: How a camera becomes a pointer
author: LuminaBoard demo lesson

pages.title: How a camera becomes a pointer
pages.text:
LuminaBoard turns a wall, a webcam and a coloured marker into an interactive board.

- 5 ideas, 5 pages: pixels, colour, finding the marker, mapping to the board, smoothing
- Use the Next / Previous controls at the bottom of the board (left click with the remote)
- Everything written on a page stays there when you come back
- Press M or right-click for the menu
pages.notes: Introduce the project goal and show how the page controls work.

pages.title: 1. What the camera really gives us
pages.text:
A picture is a grid of numbers.

- Each pixel stores Blue, Green and Red
- Each value is 0 to 255
- A 1280 x 720 frame is 921 600 pixels
- Everything that follows is arithmetic on this grid
pages.notes: OpenCV stores channels in B, G, R order.

pages.title: 2. Colour is easier in HSV
pages.text:
RGB mixes colour and brightness; HSV separates them.

- H: which colour (0 to 179 in OpenCV)
- S: how vivid
- V: how bright
> keep pixels with H in [h1, h2], S >= s1, V >= v1
- A marker keeps its hue when the light changes
pages.notes: Red wraps around hue 0, so it needs two ranges.

pages.title: 3. Finding the marker
pages.text:
Threshold, clean, then measure.

- Opening removes specks, closing fills holes
- Connected components give one blob per object
- The biggest convincing blob is the marker
> cx = m10 / m00     cy = m01 / m00
pages.notes: The centroid is the average position of the white pixels.

pages.title: 4. From camera pixels to the board
pages.text:
The camera sees the board at an angle.

- Click the 4 corners once: this is calibration
- 4 point pairs give 8 equations for the 8 unknowns of H
> [x' y' w']^T = H [x y 1]^T ,  board = (x'/w', y'/w')
- Then every camera pixel has a board position
pages.notes: Solved with the DLT algorithm and an SVD.

pages.title: 5. Smoothing the pointer
pages.text:
A raw centroid jitters by a few pixels.

- Blend each new measurement with the previous position
> p(t) = alpha * m(t) + (1 - alpha) * p(t-1)
- Small alpha: smooth but slow;  alpha = 1: raw
- Jumps are checked before they are accepted

pages.title: Your turn
pages.text:
Try the tools on this page.

- Switch to Drawing mode and write your answer here
- Why does a red marker need two hue ranges?
- Go back to page 3 with Previous and circle the centroid
- Come back: your notes are still on the page
- Menu > Image lets you zoom and pan
pages.notes: Hue is circular: red is at both ends of the scale.
